explain: Decryption needs the per-session secrets that only the two endpoints know. A key log file from your own machine contains only your own sessions. Wireshark's TLS wiki says RSA private-key decryption does not work with TLS 1.3 or with (EC)DHE key exchange. And beyond the technical answer, reading a colleague's traffic needs authorisation.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: What TLS still reveals, and fingerprinting clients with JA3
question: A TLS 1.3 connection with Encrypted Client Hello crosses your sensor. Which statement is true?
options: You can still read the real server name from the outer ClientHello's SNI
ECH encrypts the IP addresses as well
The real server name and ALPN are encrypted; the outer hello names only the client-facing server, and the server's certificate is encrypted too
ECH only works with TLS 1.2
explain: RFC 9849 encrypts the inner ClientHello (including SNI and ALPN) and the outer hello carries the public_name of the client-facing server. TLS 1.3 already encrypts certificates. IP addresses are untouched, which is why the RFC says ECH alone does not hide the server's identity.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: DNS as a control channel: tunnels, generated names and SUNBURST
question: SUNBURST waited a random 1 to 3 minutes, or 30 to 120 minutes, between DNS lookups. Which detection approach suits that best?
options: Timing regularity alone, because the waits are perfectly periodic
Blocking all DNS queries longer than 20 characters
Per-domain analysis: a rare domain receiving a unique subdomain on every query from one server, plus CNAME answers
Looking for port 53 traffic on non-standard ports
explain: The mixture of random waits from minutes to hours defeats regularity scoring. The DGA, by contrast, must produce a fresh name per query under one parent domain, which per-domain counting exposes. Blocking long names would break many legitimate services, and SUNBURST used normal DNS through the normal resolver.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Layers: the OSI and TCP/IP models, and why both exist
question: A frame crosses three routers on its way to a server. Which header is replaced at every hop, and which travels end to end?
options: The IP header is replaced at every hop; the Ethernet header travels end to end
Both are replaced at every hop
Neither changes; routers only read headers
The Ethernet (link) header is replaced at every hop; the IP header travels end to end, apart from small fields like the hop counter
explain: Link-layer addresses only mean something on one link, so each router builds a new frame for the next link. The IP addresses stay the same from source to destination (address translation, lesson 7, is the big exception). The router does change a few IP fields, such as the hop counter TTL you will meet in lesson 6.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ports, sockets and NAT
question: Which 5-tuple field is usually different for two browser tabs connected to the same HTTPS server from one laptop?
options: The source port
The destination port
The protocol
The destination IP
explain: Both tabs talk TCP to the same server address on port 443. The OS gives each connection its own ephemeral source port, which is what keeps the two byte streams apart.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTPS and TLS at a glance: what encryption hides and what it does not
question: An analyst can no longer read HTTP bodies since the company moved to HTTPS. Which question can they still answer from network data alone?
options: Which internal laptop connected to which external server name, when, and how much data moved
Which password a user typed on a login form
Which file path the user downloaded
What the session cookie value was
explain: Addresses, ports, timing and volumes are in the IP and TCP headers, and the server name is in the DNS query and the SNI. The password, path and cookie are inside the encrypted HTTP message.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
question: Thread A (node 0) and thread B (node 1) each write half of the same 4 KiB page first, at nearly the same moment. Where does the page live?
options: On whichever node's thread faulted first; the other thread's half is remote
Split: 2 KiB on each node
On both nodes, as a coherent copy per node
explain: A page is the smallest unit of placement. The first fault allocates the whole page on the faulting CPU's node, and the second thread then accesses it remotely. Give each thread page-aligned slices to avoid this.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
question: An API server's threads are spread over both nodes and the scheduler often moves them. Each request touches small, short-lived data. What is a reasonable default?
options: Pin every thread and bind all memory to node 0
Leave the default local policy, and consider automatic NUMA balancing rather than hand placement
Interleave all memory with numactl --interleave=all
explain: Short-lived per-request data is usually allocated and used by the same thread, so local allocation already places it well. Hard pinning removes scheduler flexibility, and binding to one node wastes the other controller. Hand tuning pays off for large, long-lived data.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
question: An NVMe I/O completion queue was created with 256 slots. What is the maximum number of completion entries it can hold before the controller must stop posting?
explain: The queue is full when head equals tail plus one, so one slot is always unused: 256 - 1 = 255. The spec says so explicitly: one slot in each queue is not available due to the head and tail pointer definition.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
question: A detector outputs two boxes on the same cat, both with IoU 0.9 against it. Under COCO matching, how are they scored?
options: Both are true positives
The higher-scoring one is a TP and the other is a FP
Both are false positives because the match is ambiguous
They are averaged into one detection
explain: Detections are matched in score order and each ground-truth box can be matched only once. The first takes the cat; the second has no unmatched ground truth left, so it is a false positive. This is why duplicates hurt AP.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing
question: Why does SlateDB write each manifest version as a new numbered object (00...02.manifest, 00...03.manifest) instead of overwriting one manifest key?
options: S3 cannot overwrite objects
With create-if-absent on the next number, two writers cannot both install version N+1; a plain overwrite of one key is last writer wins
Numbered objects are cheaper to PUT
LIST is only consistent for new keys
explain: S3 can overwrite, and LIST is strongly consistent, but concurrent unconditional PUTs to one key resolve as last writer wins, silently losing an update. A conditional create on the next ID means exactly one of two racing writers succeeds, which is a compare-and-swap on the database state.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Cardinality: labels multiply, and a histogram multiplies again
question: Which single change cuts the series count the most for a histogram with 11 finite buckets and 24,000 label sets?
options: Halving the number of buckets
Replacing the histogram with a summary exposing three quantiles
Dropping the instance label, 50 values, by aggregating before storage
Shortening the metric name
explain: Dropping a 50-value label divides the series count by 50. Halving the buckets takes 14 series per label set down to 8, under a factor of 2, and destroys the resolution you need for percentiles. A three-quantile summary is 5 series per label set rather than 14, a factor of under 3, and it costs you the ability to aggregate at all. The metric name has no effect on series count.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
question: What does a CTC-trained recognizer need as training labels for each cropped line image?
options: A bounding box around every character
The frame index where each character starts
A segmentation mask of each glyph
Only the transcript string of the line
explain: CTC sums over all alignments that collapse to the transcript, so the model learns alignment on its own. This is the property CRNN highlights: train from images and label sequences with no character-level annotation.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The reference monitor: one checker that sees every access
question: A driver bug lets any process overwrite kernel memory, including the code that checks permissions. Which reference monitor condition fails first?
options: Tamper proof
Fail-safe defaults
Least privilege
Small enough to verify
explain: The monitor itself can be altered by a subject. Once that is possible, nothing it decides can be trusted, which is why kernel memory bugs are so severe.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Dropping privileges correctly, and sudo's Baron Samedit
question: A daemon calls `seteuid(1000)` after startup and nothing else. An attacker gets code execution in it. What can the attacker do?
options: Nothing more than uid 1000 could
Load kernel modules, but not read files
Only read files owned by 1000
Call seteuid(0) and become root again, because the saved set-user-ID is still 0
explain: seteuid changes only the effective UID. The saved set-user-ID still holds 0, and an unprivileged process may set its effective UID to its saved one. A real drop changes all three IDs (setresuid) and then checks that setuid(0) fails.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: chroot is not a boundary, and Leaky Vessels shows why
question: Why can't an ordinary, non-root process inside a chroot use the chroot-then-cd-up trick from the man page to escape?
options: Because calling chroot itself requires CAP_SYS_CHROOT, which the process lacks
Because the kernel kills processes that call cd
Because cd .. is disabled in a chroot
It can; chroot never stops anyone
explain: The escape relies on calling chroot again. That needs CAP_SYS_CHROOT, which is why OpenSSH combines its chroot with a drop to an unprivileged user.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: What goes wrong: the confused deputy and TOCTOU races
question: A root-owned backup daemon accepts a destination path from any local user and writes the backup there with its own root authority. What is the core flaw?
options: It runs too often
It is a confused deputy: it applies its own authority to an object the caller chose, so callers can make it overwrite files they could not write
The backup is not encrypted
It should use TCP instead
explain: Hardy's compiler again. The fix is to open the destination with the caller's authority, or to have the caller hand over an open descriptor, so the daemon cannot be steered to files the caller has no right to.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
question: Why does the ICO say public availability does not end data protection duties?
options: Because public data is always copyrighted
Because individuals keep rights such as being informed even when their data was public
Because only governments may collect public data
Because the GDPR bans all web searches about people
explain: The ICO's guidance: publicly available personal data still carries the right to be informed (unless an exception applies), and collection still needs a lawful basis. It does not ban searching; it regulates processing.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Search operators: asking a search engine precise questions
question: You find an indexed spreadsheet of staff passwords on your company's site. What comes first?
options: Open it to check whether the passwords are current
Post the finding to the team chat with the link
Remove or protect the file, then rotate every credential it might contain
Ask Google to remove it, and wait
explain: Stop the exposure at the source, then assume the contents are compromised and rotate. Opening it spreads the data; de-indexing alone leaves the file reachable and the passwords valid.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Geolocation: finding where a picture was taken
question: Why look for features that would disprove your candidate location?
options: To counter confirmation bias, as the Berkeley Protocol's objectivity principle asks
Because courts require exactly ten features
To make the investigation take longer
Because satellite images are always wrong
explain: Investigators tend to see what they expect. Testing for disconfirming evidence and keeping multiple hypotheses is the Protocol's countermeasure.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Bulk collection and its ethics: the Parler archive (2021)
question: After switching to random IDs, what does OWASP say is still required for private objects?
options: An authorisation check on every object access
Nothing: random IDs are sufficient
Longer URLs
Moving to a different cloud provider
explain: OWASP's IDOR guidance treats unguessable IDs as defence in depth; access control must still be checked per object, since URLs leak.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CMake in three phases: configure, generate, build
question: A crash only happens in your Release build, and you need a debugger with line numbers but the same optimization level class. Which build type is the best first try?
options: Debug, since it has -g
RelWithDebInfo, which keeps optimization (-O2 for GCC) and adds -g
MinSizeRel, since it keeps NDEBUG
An empty CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE
explain: Debug drops optimization (only -g) and keeps asserts on, which can hide an optimizer-dependent or NDEBUG-dependent bug. RelWithDebInfo is optimized, defines NDEBUG like Release, and keeps debug info. It is still -O2 rather than Release's -O3, so the bug may move, but it is the closest standard type.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs
question: A matrix has `os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]`, `python: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]` and one `exclude` entry for `os: windows-latest, python: "3.10"`. How many jobs does the matrix create?
explain: Product $2 \times 4 = 8$, minus the one excluded combination gives 7. Each is a separate job on a separate runner.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
question: A PR fixes a real bug and adds a test, but the reviewer would have named one helper function differently and prefers a slightly different loop style that the style guide does not mention. Under Google's standard, what should the reviewer do?
options: Request changes until both points are fixed, since the PR is not yet perfect
Approve, optionally leaving the naming and loop points as Nit: comments
Close the PR and write the fix themselves in their preferred style
Approve only after a third reviewer agrees on the naming
explain: The change definitely improves code health (a fixed bug plus a test). Style points not in the style guide are personal preference, so they should not block. Marking them Nit: keeps the feedback without delaying the merge.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Why reviewer response time dominates time to merge
question: Using the model with n = 2 and F = 2, a reviewer who used to take 8 hours per response now takes 4. How much does total time to merge drop?
options: From 28 h to 24 h
From 28 h to 16 h
From 28 h to 14 h
It does not change, since the author's work is the same
explain: Total is (n+1)R + nF. Before: 3 x 8 + 4 = 28 h. After: 3 x 4 + 4 = 16 h. Each hour saved per response is saved on all three rounds, so 4 hours faster per response saves 12 hours in total.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
question: Why does QEMU decline AI-generated patches even when the contributor fully understands and tests them?
options: Because AI code is always lower quality
Because the contributor cannot confidently certify the DCO when the copyright and license status of AI output is unsettled
Because it cannot be reviewed on a mailing list
Because QEMU forbids all tools, including static analysis
explain: QEMU's concern is provenance: the Signed-off-by line certifies the DCO, and with unclear licensing of AI output the project will not take the legal risk. It explicitly allows AI use for research, debugging and static analysis whose output is not in the patch.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
question: You rebase, your IDE silently runs `git fetch` every few minutes, and a maintainer pushed to your PR branch an hour ago. You run `git push --force-with-lease`. What happens?
options: It is rejected with stale info, because the maintainer's commit is newer than your rebase
It succeeds and overwrites the maintainer's commit, because the background fetch already updated your remote-tracking ref
It succeeds and keeps both, because a lease merges the histories
It is rejected because leases cannot be used on forks
explain: A bare lease compares the remote with your remote-tracking ref. The background fetch moved that ref to the maintainer's commit, so the lease matches and the forced update goes through. `--force-if-includes` would catch this, because the commit never appeared in your branch's reflog.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: License compatibility: can these two pieces of code be combined?
question: You want to copy an Apache-2.0 function into a Linux kernel driver (GPL-2.0-only). Which is correct?
options: Allowed, Apache-2.0 is permissive so it fits any project
Allowed, if you keep the NOTICE file
Not allowed as is: the FSF does not consider Apache-2.0 compatible with GPLv2
Allowed, because the kernel has a syscall exception
explain: Apache-2.0 is compatible with GPLv3 only. Its patent termination and indemnification terms are restrictions GPLv2 does not permit, so a GPL-2.0-only work cannot absorb it. The syscall exception concerns user programs calling the kernel, not code inside it.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable
question: After `pyperf system tune` and CPU pinning, your runs vary by only 0.1%, and the patched build is 1.5% faster in every run. What can you still not conclude?
options: That the result is affected by noise
That the 1.5% comes from your change rather than a layout or order effect that favors the patched build
That the benchmark ran at all
That pyperf was installed correctly
explain: Low noise makes the gap statistically clear, but it says nothing about bias. Run order, code layout or environment size can shift one build consistently. Interleaving, rebuilding with different layouts or another machine tests for that.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Trace one request: a Redis GET from socket to reply
question: In a plugin-based web framework, `git grep -n -w handle_upload` finds only the definition and one line `routes = {"/upload": handle_upload}`. What is the best next search to find who runs it?
options: Conclude the function is dead code and propose deleting it
Search for `handle_upload(` with -w until a call appears
Search for where `routes` is read, for example `git grep -n -w routes`, to find the dispatcher that calls through the table
Search the tests for handle_upload
explain: A name stored in a table with no direct call is dynamic dispatch, as with Redis's command table. The caller looks up the table and calls the stored function, so search for the table's readers. Tests can help confirm behavior, but they do not show the production caller.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
question: Which repro is most likely to get a fast response on a library's issue tracker?
options: Your entire notebook exported as a file
A screenshot of a notebook cell and its error output
A link to a 2 GB dataset plus the 40-line script that loads it
A 3-row DataFrame built inline, the 6 lines that fail, and the full traceback
explain: Inline, artificial data plus a few failing lines and the full text traceback is copy-paste runnable. Downloads, screenshots and whole notebooks all push work onto the maintainer.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
question: Your PR moves `parser.c` into `lib/` and, while there, fixes an off-by-one in the moved function. What does the kernel guide recommend?
options: Keep both in one patch so the history shows the fix where the code now lives
Fix the bug first, then move the code in a second patch, or move first and fix second, but never modify code in the patch that moves it
Move the code and reformat it in the same patch, but put the fix separately
Leave the move out entirely; moves are never accepted
explain: The guide says not to modify moved code at all in the patch that moves it. That keeps the move verifiable as a pure move, and the fix shows up as a small, readable diff that history tools can track.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Inside the PagedAttention kernel
question: A 32-head model decodes one request with a 32,000-token context on a GPU with 108 SMs. Why does the v2 kernel, with 512-token partitions, help here?
options: It reads fewer KV bytes, because partitions skip tokens with low scores
v1 launches one thread block per head, only 32, so most SMs sit idle; v2 launches about 63 per head, roughly 2,000 in total, to spread the 32,000 keys over the whole GPU
It avoids computing the softmax, which is the slow part at long contexts
It lets heads share one copy of the keys
explain: v1's grid is (heads, sequences), so batch 1 gives 32 thread blocks, each walking 32,000 keys alone. v2 adds a partition dimension: ceil(32000/512) = 63 partitions per head. The reduce kernel's merge is exact, and the old selection rule sends any context over 8,192 tokens to v2 anyway.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
question: Which workload benefits least from prefix caching?
options: A support bot whose 3000-token system prompt is identical for every user
Multi-turn chat where each turn resends the full history
Story generation with short, unique prompts and 2000-token outputs
Many questions asked about the same uploaded report
explain: Caching only skips prefill for repeated prefixes. Unique short prompts give few hits, and with 2000-token outputs nearly all time is decode, which caching does not touch. The other three resend long identical prefixes.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: When authorisation is unclear: the Iowa courthouse arrests
question: Which single change would most directly have prevented the arrests in Iowa?
options: Using quieter lock-picking tools
Testing during a different week
Written agreement with the building's owner and advance notice to the sheriff, with a 24/7 verification number
Encrypting the final report
explain: The arrests followed from an unauthorising owner (the county) and an uninformed sheriff, plus an unreachable contact. Better tools or timing do not fix missing permission.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Active scanning: host discovery and what each probe tells you
question: A UDP scan reports port 53 as open|filtered. What does that mean?
options: A DNS server is definitely running
The port is definitely blocked
No reply came back, which happens both when a service ignores the probe and when a firewall drops it, so Nmap cannot tell which
The host is down
explain: For UDP, silence is ambiguous. Version detection, which sends a real DNS query, can turn open|filtered into open if the service answers.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Vulnerability scanners: matching versions to known flaws
question: A remote scan flags `OpenSSH 7.4` on a Red Hat Enterprise Linux server as vulnerable to several CVEs fixed in later upstream versions. A credentialed scan of the same host reports none of them. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Red Hat backported the fixes into its 7.4 package, so the banner shows an old version number while the code is patched
The credentialed scan is broken
The remote scan is always right
OpenSSH cannot be scanned remotely
explain: Enterprise distributions patch security bugs into the version they ship. Banner matching cannot see that; reading the package release from the inventory can.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Reporting: from finding to fix, and the retest
question: Which recommendation addresses a systemic issue rather than a symptom?
options: Patch Apache Struts on the dispute portal
Delete the backup directory on www
Rotate the leaked API key
Build an automatically updated software inventory and require every internet-facing system to be in it before go-live
explain: The first three fix single instances. The inventory requirement fixes the process that let unknown, unpatched systems reach the internet, which is PTES's systemic category.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Broken stacks: frame pointers, DWARF, LBR and symbols
question: A flame graph shows 25% of samples in a tower `myapp;[unknown];memcpy`, detached from the main tower. What is the most likely cause?
options: memcpy is called from an unknown thread
perf ran out of sample buffer space
memcpy was inlined
The code that called memcpy (often libc or a library) was built without frame pointers, so the walk failed
explain: A failed frame pointer walk records one junk frame as [unknown] and stops, so all those samples lose their real ancestors and pile up together. Rebuilding with frame pointers or using --call-graph dwarf restores the callers.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Publishing an update with one 8-byte store
question: Why does libpmemobj store object references as (pool id, offset) instead of virtual addresses?
options: The pool may be mapped at a different virtual address on the next run, so a saved address may be invalid
Offsets are smaller, so more fit in a cache line
Virtual addresses cannot be written with an 8-byte store
The CPU cannot flush cache lines that contain pointers
explain: Mapping addresses are chosen per run. A base-relative offset stays valid wherever the pool lands; pmemobj_direct adds the current base. PMEMoid is actually larger than a raw pointer (16 vs 8 bytes), so size is not the reason.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: The persuasion levers every lure pulls
question: Why does a written rule like 'all bank detail changes are confirmed by phone on a number we already hold' work better than training people to judge each request?
options: It makes emails load faster
It removes the need for the person to resist authority or urgency in the moment, because the rule decides
It stops attackers from sending email
It guarantees that the CEO never travels
explain: Levers work on in-the-moment judgement. A pre-committed rule takes the decision out of that moment, and using a number you already hold means the attacker cannot supply the callback number themselves.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: SPF: which servers may send for a domain
question: Which is the strongest reason SPF alone is not enough to stop a forged CEO email?
options: SPF uses too much bandwidth
SPF checks the envelope domain, not the header From the reader sees
SPF only works over IPv6
SPF requires the recipient to install a plug-in
explain: The deception lives in the header From. SPF authenticates only the MAIL FROM (and HELO) domain, which the attacker can set to a domain they control.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Lookalike domains and homoglyphs
question: Which domain is actually controlled by whoever registered 'login-verify.net'?
options: login-verify.corp.example
corp.example
corp.example.login-verify.net
verify.corp.example
explain: Read right to left: corp.example.login-verify.net is a subdomain of login-verify.net, so its owner controls it. The other three are under corp.example.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Business email compromise and invoice fraud
question: Which mailbox artefact most strongly suggests an account takeover aimed at invoice fraud?
options: A rule named '.' that moves mail containing 'invoice' to RSS Feeds
A rule moving newsletters to a 'Reading' folder
An out-of-office auto-reply
A signature block with a phone number
explain: Burying payment-related mail in a folder nobody reads, under a name chosen to look blank, keeps the real account owner from seeing replies about the fraud. MITRE lists such hiding rules as T1564.008.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
question: What is `sizeof(struct T)` for `struct T { int i; char c; };` on x86-64?
explain: i is at 0 (4 bytes), c at 4, so the data ends at 5. The struct alignment is 4 (from int), so the size rounds up to 8. The 3 bytes of tail padding keep `i` aligned in every element of a `struct T` array.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Byte order: reading and writing multi-byte fields on the wire
question: A little-endian host reads the big-endian 4-byte field `00 00 01 00` (the value 256) with a plain `memcpy` into a `uint32_t` and no conversion. What value does it get?
explain: Little-endian means the first byte is least significant: 0x00 + 0x00 x 2^8 + 0x01 x 2^16 + 0x00 x 2^24 = 65536. The bytes are right; their weights are reversed.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
question: A gym camera sees a tight group of three people, and the person detector returns only two boxes because NMS suppressed one overlapping box. What does a top-down pose system output?
options: Three skeletons, because the keypoint network sees all joints in the crop
Two skeletons; the suppressed person gets no pose at all
Three skeletons, but the third has low scores
Zero skeletons, because the boxes overlap
explain: The keypoint network only runs on boxes the detector returned. A person lost at the detection stage is lost for good: this is the early commitment problem of top-down methods.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: What a quantum computer breaks, and what it only dents
question: Which of these must be replaced because of Shor's algorithm?
options: AES-256-GCM encrypting a database
SHA-256 in a software bill of materials
ECDSA P-256 signatures on your TLS certificates
HMAC-SHA256 on API requests
explain: ECDSA rests on the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm, which Shor solves. The other three are symmetric primitives that Grover only dents, and NIST rates them as still adequate.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Lattices from zero: points, bases and hard problems
question: Why does adding small errors to random linear equations make the secret hard to find?
options: Errors make the equations inconsistent, so no secret exists
Errors make the numbers too large to store
Elimination has to combine many equations, and the combined errors grow until the answer is hidden; no efficient method is known
The errors are encrypted with AES
explain: A secret still satisfies every equation up to small errors, so it exists. What breaks is the efficient algorithm: combining equations amplifies the noise, and the best known attacks are lattice algorithms that take exponential time in the dimension.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: ML-DSA: lattice signatures that sometimes start over
question: Why does ML-DSA signing sometimes throw away its work and start over?
options: The random number generator failed
A candidate response z (or a related value) is too large, and publishing it would leak information about the secret vectors; rejection keeps signatures independent of the key
The message was too long
The context string was invalid
explain: This is the 'aborts' in Fiat-Shamir with aborts. Only responses inside a safe range are released; FIPS 204 lists the expected number of attempts per parameter set.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Crypto inventory and agility: finding every RSA before 2030
question: Which design best supports crypto agility for stored encrypted files?
options: Hard-code ML-KEM-768 everywhere so nobody can choose a weak algorithm
Let each client choose any algorithm it likes
Store an algorithm identifier with each file and route all encryption through one registry driven by a policy file
Re-encrypt every file whenever the policy changes
explain: Identifiers keep old files readable, the registry keeps the code in one place, and a policy file makes retirement a configuration change. Free client choice invites downgrades; hard-coding just recreates the RSA problem with a new name.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
question: Why does Lucene abandon the graph once it has visited more nodes than there are matching documents?
options: A flat scan costs one distance per match, a bound the walk has already exceeded, and it is exact
Lucene graphs cannot hold more nodes than the filter matches
Visiting too many nodes corrupts the HNSW index
The kNN filter is converted into a post_filter
explain: Brute force costs one distance per matching document. Once the walk has spent more distance computations than that, the graph is doing worse than a scan would, so Lucene switches to a plan with a known, bounded cost that is also exact.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Multi-tenancy: partition, shard or filter
question: Why does the pgvector README recommend list partitioning by tenant instead of one HNSW index with WHERE tenant_id = X?
options: Partitioned tables cannot be post-filtered
A shared approximate index lets one tenant's vectors affect another's recall and speed; per-tenant partitions give each tenant its own index
pgvector cannot build HNSW indexes on tables with more than one tenant
List partitioning compresses vectors
explain: In a shared index, a small tenant's rows are a tiny fraction of the candidates the scan produces, so post-filtering returns few rows and iterative scans must read far. A partition per tenant means each search runs on that tenant's own index, unfiltered.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Software prefetch: distance, hints and the kernel's lesson
question: Spot the problem: `for (p = head; p; p = p->next) { __builtin_prefetch(p->next); work(p); }` on a list of 3 nodes that is walked millions of times.
options: It can crash when p->next is NULL
The prefetch needs locality 0 to be legal
Nothing: the hardware ignores prefetches of NULL at no cost
Distance 1 is too short to hide a miss behind `work`, and on every walk the last prefetch targets NULL, which Intel says can cause long delays
explain: This is the kernel's list pattern. A prefetch never faults, so there is no crash, but one hop ahead hides little latency on a short list, and the NULL prefetch at the end of every walk was measured at about 20 cycles. The kernel removed these prefetches.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Pseudonyms and hashes are not anonymity: AOL 2006
question: AOL replaced usernames with random numbers. Why did that not protect Thelma Arnold?
options: The pseudonym linked all of one person's queries, and the queries themselves pointed to a town, a surname and a neighbourhood
The random numbers were guessable
The data was not encrypted at rest
AOL included IP addresses
explain: The number did its job of hiding the username. But it grouped hundreds of queries from one person, and their content (place, surname, neighbourhood) identified them. Content can be a quasi-identifier.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy: a promise about one person
question: A mechanism is 0.5-DP. You run it three times on the same data and publish all three answers. What guarantee do the three answers together have?
options: 0.5-DP, since each answer is 0.5-DP
0.167-DP, since the noise averages out
No guarantee at all
1.5-DP, by composition
explain: Basic composition adds the epsilons: 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.5. Averaging the three answers is post-processing of that combined release, so it is also 1.5-DP, not better.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Designing for less: data minimisation and purpose limitation
question: A product team wants to store full birth dates 'to personalise birthday offers', but the offer only needs the month. What does data minimisation imply?
options: Store the full date but encrypt it
Store the full date and delete it after one year
Store only the birth month, since the purpose does not need more
Ask users for consent to store the full date
explain: Minimisation means limited to what is necessary for the purpose. The month achieves the purpose; the full date is a strong quasi-identifier with no use here. Encryption or consent do not make unnecessary data necessary.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Data protection impact assessments that change the design
question: A team launches a feature, then writes a DPIA three months later 'for the file'. What is the main problem?
options: DPIAs must be written by lawyers
DPIAs expire after three months
Only regulators may write DPIAs
Article 35 requires the assessment prior to the processing, so its findings can still change the design
explain: The duty applies before processing starts, and the point is to change the design while that is cheap. An after-the-fact DPIA can still help, but the launch was out of line with Article 35.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 1: reading sudo rules like an auditor
question: A sudo rule allows `/opt/app/bin/rotate.sh` as root. The file is owned by root with mode 755, but `/opt/app/bin` is owned by the app user, who holds the rule. Is the rule safe?
options: Yes, the file is owned by root and not writable by others
No: whoever can write the directory can rename the file and put their own rotate.sh in its place
Yes, because sudo checks the file's owner before running it
Only if NOPASSWD is removed
explain: Write permission on a directory lets you create, delete and rename entries in it (linux-for-security). The app user can replace rotate.sh with a new file. sudo does not check ownership of the target by default, so the directory must be root-owned too.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Windows escalation 2: AlwaysInstallElevated and token privileges
question: An attacker uploads a web shell to an IIS server; it runs as the app pool identity. Why do defenders treat this as close to SYSTEM compromise?
options: App pool identities are members of Administrators
IIS runs every request as SYSTEM
Web shells disable UAC
Service identities hold SeImpersonatePrivilege by default, which turns a connecting SYSTEM client into SYSTEM code
explain: Processes started as services get the Service group and with it SeImpersonatePrivilege. If the attacker can make a privileged client connect to something they control, impersonation gives them that client's rights. That is why web servers need patching, least-privilege identities and process-tree alerting.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Discovery: how intruders map a network, and why it is noisy
question: backup01 triggers the fan-out alert every night. What is the best response?
options: Raise the global threshold to 30
Delete the rule; it is too noisy
Allowlist backup01 for its known role and destinations, keep the rule for everything else, and monitor backup01 itself closely
Block backup01 from using SMB
explain: The alert is correct but expected for that role. A targeted exception keeps the signal for every other host. Raising the threshold would also have hidden laptop7, and blocking the backup server breaks backups.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: How a PRM is trained and how it scores a solution
question: Why did Lightman et al. surface 'convincing wrong-answer' solutions to labelers instead of random samples?
options: They are guaranteed to contain a step the current PRM misjudged, so each label corrects a real mistake
They are shorter, so labeling is cheaper
Random samples cannot be split into steps
It removes the need to label correct solutions at all
explain: A solution the PRM rates highly but whose answer is wrong must contain at least one step the PRM scored too high. Labeling it is maximally informative. This active learning was about 2.6x more data-efficient in their ablation.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL
question: In process-supervised GRPO, two outputs have identical first steps with the same PRM reward. Why can their first-step tokens get opposite-sign advantages?
options: Normalization uses a different mean per output
The KL penalty differs between the outputs
Each token's advantage sums the normalized rewards of its own step and all later steps, so later steps differ
Only the last step's reward matters
explain: The advantage for a token is the sum of normalized step rewards at or after its step. In the example both first steps normalize to 0.77, but output 2's later step (-1.92) makes its first-step advantage -1.15.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Linux: every thread is a task, and clone() picks what to share
question: A thread in a 4-thread web server calls `chdir("/tmp")`, then another thread opens the relative path `log.txt`. Where does the file get opened?
options: In /tmp, because pthreads share CLONE_FS state such as the working directory
In the old working directory, because each thread keeps its own cwd
It depends on which CPU each thread runs on
The open fails because cwd changes are not allowed in multi-threaded programs
explain: pthread_create passes CLONE_FS, so the working directory is shared by all threads of the process. This is a real source of bugs: a library that calls chdir silently changes path resolution for every thread.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Who runs next: run queues, CFS, EEVDF and nice
question: A bug puts a `SCHED_FIFO` priority 50 thread into an infinite loop that never blocks, on a machine with default settings. Why can a normal shell on the same CPU still run, slowly?
options: SCHED_FIFO threads are preempted after a 0.7 ms slice like everyone else
The shell's nice value outranks real-time priority
EEVDF gives the shell an earlier virtual deadline
Starvation protection: by default normal tasks are guaranteed about 5 percent of each CPU (50 ms of every 1 s)
explain: Real-time threads always beat normal ones and SCHED_FIFO has no time slice, so without a safety net the loop would starve the CPU. Older kernels reserve it with RT throttling (sched_rt_runtime_us 950,000 of 1,000,000 us, as sched(7) documents); since Linux 6.12 a fair deadline server gives normal tasks 50 ms of every 1 s on each CPU, the default protection from 7.2 on.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Training per-slice codebooks and encoding a vector
question: A colleague trains one PQ codebook per sub-vector but forgets to use the same dimension split at encoding time (they split the database vectors in a different order). What happens?
options: Nothing, because k-means is permutation invariant
Codes are still valid but 2x larger
Every sub-vector is matched against a codebook learned on different dimensions, so reconstructions and distances are garbage
Only the first sub-vector is affected
explain: Codebook C_j only knows the distribution of slice j. Feeding it a different slice produces arbitrary nearest-centroid choices. The split (and any rotation applied before it) is part of the model and must be identical for training, encoding and querying.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Inner product, cosine and ScaNN's anisotropic quantization
question: Two codewords reconstruct a unit-norm database vector x with the same squared error. Codeword A's error lies along x, codeword B's is orthogonal to x. For maximum inner product search with T = 0.2, which does ScaNN's loss prefer?
options: A, because error along x keeps the direction of x intact
Either: the errors are equal, so the losses are equal
Neither: ScaNN only uses the threshold during search
B, because parallel error is weighted eta = 4.125 times more and changes the scores of high-scoring queries most
explain: Queries that score high with x point roughly along it, so their inner product with the error picks up the parallel part almost fully and the orthogonal part barely. The loss weights parallel error by eta (4.125 at T = 0.2, d = 100), so B is preferred even though plain reconstruction error ties.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: DSPy: signatures, modules and optimizers
question: Your RAG program has a query-writer predictor and an answer predictor, but your data only labels final answers. How does BootstrapFewShot get demos for the query writer?
options: It cannot; you must hand-label good queries
It runs the whole program, and when the final answer passes the metric it keeps every predictor's input and output from that run as demos
It asks the proposer LLM to invent ideal queries without running the program
It fine-tunes the query writer on the answers
explain: Bootstrapping keeps full traces of runs that pass the metric, so intermediate steps get demos for free. That is the main reason DSPy needs labels only for the final output.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Twenty letters, one backbone: the design problem
question: Why does the many-to-one map from sequence to structure help a design pipeline?
options: It means each backbone has exactly one correct sequence, so the search is easy
It means structure prediction is impossible, so designs must be tested in the lab
It means many sequences fold to nearly the same backbone, so you can sample several per backbone and keep the ones that validate
It means the backbone can be ignored once the sequence is chosen
explain: Many sequences map to nearly the same fold. That redundancy is what makes sampling 8 (or 100) sequences per backbone and filtering them a sensible strategy, rather than needing to find the one true sequence.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: The funnel: from 100 backbones to a binder that works
question: Which statement about the two-stage pipeline is correct?
options: The backbone generator and the sequence designer are trained jointly, end to end, on experimental binding data
ProteinMPNN generates the backbone and RFdiffusion assigns the sequence
AlphaFold2 is used to generate candidate backbones, and RFdiffusion filters them
The backbone generator never sees a sequence, the sequence designer never changes the backbone, and a structure predictor is the referee between them
explain: The three models are trained separately and composed at inference. RFdiffusion places frames with no sequence, ProteinMPNN writes a sequence for fixed backbone coordinates, and AF2 or ESMFold judges whether the sequence folds back to the backbone. Nothing in the loop is trained on the assay results.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
question: You change one byte at the very end of a 2 GB file. How much of its SHA-256 digest changes?
options: About half of the bits, so it looks like a completely unrelated digest
Only the last hex digit or two
Nothing, because SHA-256 samples only the start of large files
The digest length grows by one byte
explain: Cryptographic hashes are designed so that any change to the input flips about half the output bits, unpredictably. The digest length is always fixed (64 hex digits for SHA-256), and every byte of the input counts.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Turning a script into a command-line tool with argparse
question: Why does the file end with `if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main())` instead of just `sys.exit(main())`?
options: So that importing authscan from a test runs no code and does not exit the test runner
It makes the script run faster
Because argparse requires it
So the script only works on Linux
explain: Importing a module runs its top-level code. Without the guard, `from authscan import scan` in a test file would parse the test runner's own arguments and call sys.exit. The guard is true only when the file is executed directly.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
question: A rule `personal computer => pc` is used at search time. A user types `personal computer`; a document contains only `personal computer`, never `pc`. What happens?
options: It matches, because explicit rules keep both sides
It does not match through the synonym: the query is rewritten to pc, and the document was indexed without that rule
It matches only with expand: false
The analyzer rejects the rule because multi-word left sides are invalid
explain: An explicit rule replaces the left side with the right side. Applied only at search time, the query becomes pc, which this document does not contain. Use an equivalent rule (personal computer, pc) or include the original on the right side if both should match.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Expanding with models: doc2query, query2doc and HyDE
question: Why does query2doc repeat the query 5 times before appending the pseudo-document for BM25?
options: To keep the original terms from being outweighed by the much longer generated passage
To raise the query's IDF
Because BM25 ignores terms that appear only once in a query
To force the LLM to stay on topic
explain: BM25 over a long concatenated query is a sum over many terms; without repetition the passage's words dominate. Repeating q is a weight on the original terms, like the 0.5 weight on synonyms or RM3's original query weight.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Rewrite-Retrieve-Read: training a rewriter on the reader's feedback
question: Why does the reward include a Hit term (+1 if the answer string appears in the retrieved text, -1 otherwise) besides EM and F1?
options: It directly rewards retrieving useful evidence, even when the reader fails to use it
It replaces the KL penalty
It makes the reward differentiable
It penalizes long queries
explain: EM and F1 depend on the reader as well as the query. Hit isolates the rewriter's own job, getting the answer into the retrieved context, so a good query is rewarded even if the frozen reader misreads the passage.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Binary search plus rescoring: oversample, then re-rank
question: Your binary index is in RAM and original vectors are on an SSD. Recall is too low at oversampling 2. What is the main cost of raising oversampling to 8?
options: The binary index gets 4x larger
Queries must be re-embedded
Stage 2 reads about 4x more original vectors from disk per query
The Hamming scan must use floating-point math
explain: The binary scan cost barely changes. Stage 2 work, mostly random SSD reads of original vectors, grows with the number of candidates, so going from 2k to 8k candidates is about 4x more reads.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ inside an index: IVF clusters, graphs and fast rotations
question: A team rotates every query with a dense 1536 x 1536 matrix and serves 100,000 queries per second. What does the rotation alone cost, and what is the fix?
options: About 2.4 million multiply-adds per probed cluster per query; probe fewer clusters
Nothing measurable, since the rotation is applied only at index time
About 2.4 million multiply-adds per query, roughly 2.4 x 10^11 per second; switch to a Hadamard-based rotation such as FHT/Kac, about 53 thousand operations per query
About 1,536 multiply-adds per query; no fix needed
explain: 1536^2 = 2,359,296 multiply-adds per query, once per query (re-centering per cluster is only a subtraction). At 100k QPS that is about 2.4 x 10^11 per second just to rotate. A structured transform cuts it to O(D log D), about 44x less here, and stores 4D sign bits instead of a 9.4 MB matrix.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Build it: RaBitQ versus PQ and plain BQ on real embeddings
question: Your IVF-RaBitQ index has low recall at nprobe = 4. You raise oversampling from 1 to 4 and recall barely moves (0.635 to 0.712 on SciFact). What is the better next step?
options: Raise nprobe, since the missing neighbors are in clusters that were never scanned
Switch to a dense rotation matrix
Raise oversampling to 16
Lower the query bits from 4 to 2
explain: Rescoring only re-orders candidates from probed lists. At nprobe = 16 the same index reached 0.929 with oversampling 4. Oversampling fixes estimation error; nprobe fixes coverage.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Race conditions from zero: concurrency, the race window and TOCTOU
question: Which code shape is a TOCTOU race in a web application?
options: Reading a product description and rendering it
Hashing a password with bcrypt before storing it
Reading whether a gift card is unredeemed, then in a later statement marking it redeemed and crediting the user
Sending a confirmation email after an order has been committed
explain: The gift card code checks a state (unredeemed) and later acts on it (mark and credit) in separate steps, so two requests can both pass the check. Reading for display and hashing do not decide anything; sending an email after a commit acts on state that is already final.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Fixing races in the database: atomic updates, locks, constraints
question: Which statement correctly stops five parallel withdrawals of 100 from a balance of 100 at PostgreSQL's default isolation level?
options: SELECT balance in one statement, check it in Python, then UPDATE balance = balance - 100, all in one transaction
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 100, then check the affected row count
UPDATE accounts SET balance = :computed_value WHERE id = 1, with the value computed in Python
Running the SELECT twice to make sure the balance is still 100
explain: The conditional UPDATE re-evaluates its WHERE clause after waiting for a concurrent updater, so only one debit matches. Checking in Python and then debiting is the vulnerable read_then_debit; writing a value computed in Python is the lost update; reading twice does not close the window.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Testing logic: invariants, abuse cases and concurrency tests
question: In Kettle's predict step, why is a password reset that stores the token in the users table (keyed by user id) a poor race target, while one that stores it in the session is a good one?
options: Session storage is always slower
Users tables cannot be locked
Session tokens are shorter
Two resets for two different users write two different rows, so they never collide; two resets in one session write the same session record
explain: A collision needs two operations on the same record. Keyed by user id, parallel resets for two users touch two rows. Keyed by session, both requests overwrite the same session's username and token, which can leave them mismatched.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit
question: A 5-server cluster's leader is in term 3 with commitIndex 5. Its entries 6 to 9 all have term 3. The matchIndex values (leader included) are 9, 9, 8, 6, 5. What is the new commitIndex?
explain: Sorted descending: 9, 9, 8, 6, 5. The middle value 8 is stored on three servers (two with 9, one with 8), a majority of 5, and entry 8 has the current term. Index 9 is on only two servers. So commitIndex becomes 8, which also commits 6 and 7.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Indexing: how chunk size and overlap decide what can be found
question: You switch from 1024-token chunks to 256-token chunks and keep top-k at 2. What is the most likely new problem?
options: Each chunk's embedding becomes vaguer, so precision drops
The prompt overflows the context window
The LLM now sees a quarter as much text, so answers that span several sentences may lose a needed piece
Overlap stops working because it only applies to large chunks
explain: Smaller chunks give sharper embeddings, but 2 chunks of 256 tokens is 512 tokens of evidence instead of 2048. That is why the LlamaIndex example doubles top-k when it halves chunk size. Our toy shows the same thing: with 12-word chunks the 6 weeks chunk sits at rank 4.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: The seven failure points and how to debug them
question: A user asks for the refund policy as a bulleted list. The answer is correct and grounded but comes back as one paragraph. Which failure point is this?
options: FP 5 Wrong Format
FP 4 Not Extracted
FP 7 Incomplete
FP 2 Missed the Top Ranked Documents
explain: The facts are present and right; only the requested format was ignored. Barnett et al. define FP 5 as the LLM ignoring an instruction to extract information in a certain format such as a table or list.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
question: Which feature is most likely to be inflated by position bias?
options: Title BM25
Query-URL click count
URL length
Document age
explain: Click counts depend on where the document was shown: top results get examined and clicked more even when a lower result is more relevant, as the swapped-order experiment showed. The other three do not depend on past rankings.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: nDCG precisely: gain, discount, log base and the ideal
question: A run's grade 3 document at rank 1 and grade 1 document at rank 4 swap places. Which raw DCG@5 variant drops more?
options: Linear gain, because it is proportional to the grade
Neither, because DCG ignores grades beyond binary relevance
Exponential gain, because it makes the grade 3 worth 7 instead of 3
They drop equally, because only the discounts change
explain: The swap costs (gain difference) x (1 - 0.431), where 1 and 0.431 are the discounts of ranks 1 and 4 (0.431 is 1 / log2 5). Linear gain: 2 x 0.569 = 1.14. Exponential gain: (7 - 1) x 0.569 = 3.41. Exponential gain amplifies anything involving the top grade, which is why it is preferred when a few excellent results matter most.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? Paired tests, effect sizes, many systems
question: You compare 8 rankers pairwise with 28 independent paired t-tests at alpha = 0.05 and find 2 significant differences. What is the main concern?
options: With 28 tests, the chance of at least one false positive is about 0.76, so 2 hits are weak evidence; use ANOVA plus a multiple comparison test such as randomised Tukey HSD
The t-test cannot be used with paired data
The Wilcoxon test would have been more accurate
Nothing; each test is valid on its own
explain: 1 - 0.95^28 is about 0.76, so finding a couple of significant pairs is close to what chance alone would produce. Sakai suggests testing all systems together first and then applying a multiple comparison procedure. Smucker et al. found Wilcoxon less reliable, not more.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: The way in: brokers, stolen logins and edge devices
question: A help desk agent resets MFA for a caller who knows the employee's name, ID and manager. Which control from the script closes this route?
options: MFA everywhere
Patching KEV vulnerabilities
Killing VPN sessions
Strong caller verification at the help desk
explain: The route does not attack the login technology; it asks a person to issue a new factor. Only a verification process that an attacker with public or stolen facts cannot pass (for example a call-back to a number on file, or approval by the manager) closes it.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Inside a crew: what the Conti playbook taught defenders
question: Why does the hunt escalate SRV-FILE-1 but only review SRV-APP-4?
options: SRV-FILE-1 is a file server and those are always critical
SRV-FILE-1 shows three different stages of the playbook in a few hours; SRV-APP-4 shows one tool
GMER is less dangerous than AdFind
SRV-APP-4 is on the allowlist
explain: Combining stages raises confidence, as correlation rules in the logging course did: discovery, persistence and exfiltration together form the attack chain. A single tool may be explainable; it is still reviewed, not ignored.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Recovery sequencing: identity first, then the business
question: Microsoft recommends restoring AD from a backup taken a few days before the failure rather than the latest one. Why?
options: The most recent backup may contain the attacker's changes, so a slightly older one trades some lost data for a lower risk of reintroducing them
Older backups are smaller
Recent backups cannot be restored on new hardware
Tombstone lifetime forbids recent backups
explain: The guide calls it a trade-off between recency and safety. Changes after the backup are lost, but a backup from inside the compromise window can bring back backdoor accounts and permissions.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
question: A cache server registers each 4 KB request buffer just before using it and deregisters it after. Throughput is poor. What is the best fix?
options: Use RDMA READ instead of WRITE
Register one large pool at startup, preferably on huge pages, and reuse buffers from it
Disable the protection domain
Use more QPs
explain: Registration enters the kernel and pins pages, so per-request registration puts the slow control path back on the data path. Registering a pool once fixes that, and large pages keep the NIC's translation cache small (FaRM's lesson).

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
question: Your RC QP has `timeout = 14` and `retry_cnt = 7`. A peer machine loses power mid-transfer. What does the sender see, and roughly when?
options: Nothing; the WR stays pending forever
An IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR completion after on the order of half a second, with the QP in an error state
An RNR error immediately
A TCP reset
explain: With no ACKs, the NIC retries after each 67.1 ms timeout; once retry_cnt is exhausted the WR completes with IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR (about 8 x 67 ms = 537 ms in the simple model). RNR is about missing receive buffers on a live peer, not a dead one.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
question: A Colyseus room has 200 entities and you call `sort()` on their ArraySchema every tick to keep a leaderboard ordered. Bandwidth spikes. Why?
options: Sorting changes refIds, which forces a full resync
Schemas cannot hold more than 63 entities
sort() marks every index as changed, so the whole array is re-sent every patch
Sorted arrays disable delta encoding for the whole room
explain: The Colyseus optimization docs: sort() re-sends every element because every index is marked changed. Sort a plain copy on the client, or sort a separate array of indexes, instead.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
question: Why does the identity Y transpose C Y = Y transpose Y + Y transpose (C - I) Y, with C user u's diagonal confidence matrix, matter?
options: It makes the loss convex in X and Y jointly
It lets each user update cost depend on that user's n_u touched items instead of all n items, so a sweep is linear in the number of non-zeros
It removes the need for regularization
It turns ALS into SGD
explain: Y transpose Y is shared and precomputed once per sweep. The user-specific correction only involves rows with c_ui different from 1, which are the items the user touched.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why one pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo
question: When is a single pixels-per-mm ratio from the card exact for an object on the same table?
options: Whenever the card and the object are both fully visible
When you average the ratios from all four edges
When the image plane is parallel to the table, so every table point has the same depth
When the object is shorter than the card
explain: With the camera looking straight at the plane, every point on it has the same Z, so f/Z is one constant. Averaging edges or keeping the object short reduces nothing about perspective; only a fronto-parallel view (image plane parallel to the table) makes the ratio constant (ignoring lens distortion).

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory
question: Which input should a hash join normally build its hash table on?
options: The larger input, so probing is cheaper
Whichever comes first in the FROM clause
The input that is already sorted
The smaller input, so the table fits in memory
explain: Build cost and memory grow with the build side, while each probe is a constant-time lookup either way. Building on the smaller input keeps the table in memory and avoids batching. In the docs' plan the Hash node sits over the 100-row tenk1 scan, not the 10000-row tenk2.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leaderless quorums: why R + W > N makes reads overlap writes
question: N = 5 with R = 4, W = 2. Reads always overlap the last write, yet two clients writing the same key at the same time can both succeed without either write reaching a replica that has the other. Why?
options: Because R + W = 6 is too close to N
Because W = 2 is not a majority of 5, so two write sets can be disjoint
Because reads with R = 4 cannot tolerate failures
Because coordinators send writes to only W replicas
explain: Read/write overlap needs $R + W > N$. Write/write overlap needs $2W > N$. Two sets of 2 fit disjointly inside 5 replicas, so concurrent writers cannot detect each other through a shared replica.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
question: Which of these is NOT reward hacking?
options: An agent edits the unit tests so they pass without fixing the bug
A robot moves between the camera and the object so a learned reward model thinks it grasped it
A model fails a coding task because it cannot write the algorithm, and gets reward 0
A boat circles to re-collect shaping points instead of finishing the race
explain: Reward hacking requires a high proxy score with poor true performance. A model that honestly fails gets a low proxy score that matches its true performance: that is a capability gap, not a specification failure.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: KL regularization: a leash, not a cure
question: Gao et al. found that a KL penalty in their PPO runs did not improve the gold score reached at a given KL. Which interpretation matches their paper?
options: KL penalties make overoptimization worse
KL penalties have no effect on training
The gold RM was itself hacked
The penalty acted like early stopping: it changed where training converged, not the gold-versus-KL frontier
explain: Gold scores depended only on the KL reached; the penalty made training converge earlier on the same frontier. They also caution the result may be sensitive to hyperparameters, and Coste et al. found a small KL penalty useful when combined with RM ensembles.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Catching hacks: CoT monitors, obfuscation, generalization
question: Your RL task family scores each episode pass or fail, capped at 1. Which of the detection signals in this lesson stops working there?
options: Inspecting anomalously high-scoring runs, since every pass scores the same 1
LLM monitors reading the transcript
Diff inspection of changed files
Hidden tests
explain: METR notes the high-score heuristic does not work for HCAST tasks for exactly this reason: with binary, capped scores a hack cannot score higher than an honest pass. They used an LLM monitor there instead. Diffs and hidden tests do not depend on the score's range.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Monte Carlo: simulating 100,000 years of losses
question: Why does the code draw a fresh TEF and vulnerability for every simulated year instead of fixing them once?
options: To make the program slower
Because PERT only works for one draw
Because the Poisson function requires it
Because the true values are uncertain, and drawing them each year spreads that uncertainty into the result
explain: The ranges express uncertainty about the inputs themselves. Sampling them per iteration propagates that uncertainty into the loss distribution; fixing them would understate the spread.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: SOC 2: trust services criteria, Type I vs II, and your evidence
question: During a Type II period, an engineer merges a hotfix without review under pressure during an outage. What should happen so the audit treats it correctly?
options: Delete the commit history
Nothing; auditors do not look at hotfixes
Follow the documented emergency change procedure: record the reason, get a retrospective review and approval soon after, and keep the ticket
Rewrite the change as a Type I control
explain: Emergency changes are normal; undocumented ones are exceptions. A defined emergency process with retrospective approval is a control the auditor can test.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: EU law for engineers: GDPR, NIS2, DORA and the Cyber Resilience Act
question: A database backup with customer emails is found on a public bucket. It was encrypted with a key stored only in your KMS, and access logs show no downloads of the key. Under GDPR Article 34, must you notify the affected individuals?
options: Yes, always within 72 hours
No, and you need not record it anywhere
Probably not: Art. 34(3)(a) exempts data rendered unintelligible to unauthorised people, such as by encryption; still document it and assess whether the authority must be told
Only if more than 500 people are affected
explain: Encryption with an uncompromised key is the textbook Art. 34(3)(a) case. Art. 33(5) still requires documenting all breaches, and you assess risk for the Art. 33 authority notification.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
question: Your insurance application says 'MFA is enforced on all remote access'. A forgotten VPN appliance allows password-only logins, and ransomware enters through it. What is the risk?
options: None; insurance always pays
The deductible doubles automatically
The insurer may dispute or deny the claim because the declared control was not in place
Only the VPN vendor is liable
explain: The NCSC warns that if you claim measures are in place when they are not, the insurer may not be obliged to pay. Applications deserve the same accuracy as audit evidence.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
question: In the toy model, the 16,000-token response is replaced by one of 4000 tokens. What happens to the synchronous rollout time?
options: It drops to 80 s, because every engine now finishes at 4000 tokens
It drops from 320 s to 122 s, because engine 3's 6100-token response becomes the longest
It stays at 320 s, because the batch size is unchanged
It drops to about 79 s, the mean length times 20 ms
explain: A synchronous batch ends when its longest response ends. Without the 16k response the longest is 6100 tokens on engine 3, so 6100 x 20 ms = 122 s. The mean sets throughput only if nothing waits for the tail.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
question: Kimi K2 broadcasts the full parameter set to every checkpoint-engine worker, although each inference worker needs only a shard. Why accept several times more bytes?
options: Inference engines cannot accept shards, only whole checkpoints
Broadcasting compresses the weights, so it moves fewer bytes in the end
It decouples the trainer's and engine's sharding from each other, and the simpler pipelined broadcast used the bandwidth better than transfer-what-you-need
It is required for FP8 rollout
explain: The report trades bytes for simplicity: each engine slices what it needs from a complete copy, so neither engine has to know the other's layout. It also says this beat the shard-exact approach in practice because of reduced synchronization overhead and higher bandwidth utilization, giving updates under 30 s for a 1T model.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Multi-turn agentic rollouts: tools, servers and token-in, token-out
question: A multi-turn trainer stores each conversation as chat messages and re-applies the chat template to build training tokens. Why can this silently make training off-policy?
options: The chat template adds a system prompt, which doubles the loss
The re-encoded ids can differ from the sampled ids (parser edits, non-canonical splits, special tokens), so the loss scores tokens the policy never produced
Chat templates cannot represent tool calls
Re-tokenizing is too slow for training
explain: The gradient should raise or lower the probability of choices the policy actually made. If the ids differ, logprobs and masks refer to a different sequence, and the importance ratios compare two policies on tokens neither sampled. verl saw PPO fail to converge this way, hence token-in, token-out APIs.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: The four golden signals, read as distributions
question: Edge reports mean latency 188 ms, median 10 ms, p90 1025 ms. Another engineer says the edge is slow and wants to scale it. What do these three numbers actually say?
options: The edge is saturated, since the mean is 19 times the median
A minority of edge requests (about 17 percent) are extremely slow while the majority are untouched, so the fault is on a path that only some requests take
The edge has a latency distribution typical of a healthy service under load
The p90 is unreliable at this traffic level and should be ignored
explain: The median being unchanged rules out anything that affects all edge requests, and a p90 at 1025 ms with a p50 at 10 ms puts a large mass far to the right. In the model 45 percent of edge traffic enters checkout and 37 percent of those are slow, so 16.7 percent of edge requests sit at the top mode. Scaling the edge would add capacity to the part that is working.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
question: A reviewer rejects the postmortem because the Root Cause field says three things. Based on how the SRE book and Allspaw's writing treat causes, what is the better response?
options: Keep all three: complex systems fail from several conditions that are individually insufficient and jointly sufficient, which is why the field is plural and each condition gets an action item
Pick the earliest event in the timeline, since it caused the others
Pick the one with the most direct mechanism and list the others as background
Rewrite it as a chain of five whys so the single deepest cause becomes clear
explain: The troubleshooting chapter notes that multiple factors may each be insufficient yet jointly causal, Google's template says Root Causes, and Allspaw's objection to the Five Whys is precisely that a linear chain forces a single terminal cause, usually a person. Picking the earliest event or the most vivid mechanism discards the conditions whose removal would have changed the outcome.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: When score fusion beats RRF
question: An internal search fuses BM25 with a dense model. You have 300 labeled queries from real traffic, and both retrievers expose stable scores. What does the evidence suggest?
options: Tune a convex combination of normalized scores (one α) and compare it against RRF on held-out queries
